newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds jury hears late smoker's deposition.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds jury hears late smoker's deposition.

text.p: Jurors hearing a wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. on Thursday watched the videotaped testimony of a smoker who died of lung cancer 18 months ago as she detailed her struggle to quit.

Jean Connor, whose family sued the tobacco company alleging it made a defective and dangerous product, told jurors via a deposition videotaped a few months before her death that she tried to quit smoking because she wanted to have plastic surgery and her surgeon would not carry out the procedure while she smoked.
"I cut back on my cigarettes, my consumption. I cut back on the amount of my smoking. Then I went back up again," Connor said.

The six-member jury watched with rapt attention as an hour-long portion of Connor's deposition was screened on two large monitors in the Jacksonville courtroom where the closely followed case is being heard.
Connor, a bank manager and mother of three who died at age 49, appeared gaunt and wore a wig.
She said she resorted to a prescription nicotine patch in her attempt to quit smoking in 1993, several months before she was diagnosed with cancer. She died in October 1995.

Attorney Norwood "Woody" Wilner, who last summer won the largest judgment ever against a tobacco company, called Dr. Allan Feingold, the plaintiff's first and only expert witness, shortly before the trial broke for lunch.

Feingold, chief of pulmonary medicine at South Miami Hospital, was a key witness in the August 1996 trial in which Wilner won a $750,000 judgment against Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. Brown & Williamson, a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc, is appealing the judgment.
Feingold's first few minutes on the stand served notice that his testimony was likely to be contentious, as Reynolds' lawyer Paul Crist questioned his qualifications to render opinions in the case.
"We are not in the living room having an argument," Judge Bernard Nachman said at one point, ordering Crist to ask questions and telling Feingold to answer them.

In a hearing last week, Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., successfully argued that Nachman should curtail any attempt by Feingold to make extemporaneous commentary and limit him to answering lawyers' questions.
Feingold is expected to be on the witness stand for two days.
